D1 · Steve Kromer
Berkeley City Council · District 1 · November 3, 2026
# D1 is where Berkeley gets to work.
Services that work, dollars spent wisely, and a Council that sticks to the job. Below: seven things to get done, where I stand on the issues Berkeley is arguing about, and how to help. Open any card for the detail.
The seatOpen — no incumbent
The focusStreets, safety, services
How to winRank Steve #1 — or #2
Want everything on one page? See the full site.
## Seven things to get done
In priority order, the way you'd sequence a job. Every item answers two questions: what's being traded, and what gets published so you can tell whether it worked.
Full build list →
01The basics
### Core services, done right
Smooth streets, working lights, clean sidewalks, calls returned. That's the job, and it comes first.
The balance, the check, and where it's been tested
The everyday things residents pay for and too often don't get: potholes filled, trash picked up, streetlights fixed, a call that gets a call back.
The balanceA fixed budget and finite staff hours — every dollar and hour that drifts to a new initiative comes out of streets, lights, and pickups.
The checkResponse times, published monthly: pothole fills, streetlight repairs, 311 closures.
Tested: Hopkins Street →Full page →
02My record
### Spend every dollar like it's ours
Plain-language budgets, published results, and a hard line on what we pay for versus what we get.
The balance, the check, and where it's been tested
I've spent years tracking how Berkeley spends its money — building the Berkeley Transparency Hub, a public tracker of council agendas and contracts. I'll bring that scrutiny to the dais. Six departments take four out of every five dollars.
The balanceA plan you stick to against a plan you keep reopening — every priority added mid-cycle is paid for by something already promised.
The checkWhat we funded last cycle set next to what actually got finished — and published results beside every contract: what we paid, what we got.
Tested: budget vs. what was spent →Tested: Where's the scorecard? →Tested: the no-bid surveillance contract →Where the money goes →Full page →
03Cut the red tape
### A City Hall that actually answers
Faster permits, real response times, performance you can measure. For housing: fast, predictable permits for what fits the neighborhood.
The balance, the check, and where it's been tested
A bureaucracy that works for residents instead of the other way around. The same goes for housing: write the design standards first, then permit what fits them quickly and predictably, so no one needs a decade of design review to find out.
The balanceProcess buys certainty and costs time — every added week of review is paid by the applicant, the neighbor, and the housing that waits.
The checkPublished permit clocks: median days from application to decision, by permit type.
Tested: upzoning the corridors →Full page →
04Parks & safety
### Safe, clean public spaces
Competent public safety and well-kept parks — Ohlone, Cedar Rose, James Kenney, North Waterfront — maintained like we mean it.
The balance, the check, and where it's been tested
The shared spaces that make District 1 livable. Parks are where neighbors actually meet; keeping them clean and usable is the unglamorous work I want more of at City Hall.
The balanceShared spaces have to be both safe and open to everyone — enough presence to keep a park usable, enough restraint to keep it public.
The checkA published maintenance schedule and park condition reports, kept current.
Tested: tear gas — one vote, three decisions →Full page →
05Homelessness
### Oversight, coordination, results
Most of the money comes from outside the city. Make it work together, publish what it bought, fix what the counts show isn't working.
The balance, the check, and where it's been tested
Federal, state, and county dollars fund most of Berkeley's homeless services. The council's job is to make them work together and to say plainly what they bought: how many people got help, how many got indoors, and what each program delivers for what it costs.
The balanceHelp tonight against housing for good — shelter beds and permanent units draw on the same dollars, and most of those dollars answer to the state and county before they answer to Berkeley.
The checkThe counts, published: people helped, people indoors, cost per outcome, program by program.
Tested: who controls the beds? →Tested: the five dates ahead →Full page →
06West Berkeley
### Back the makers in West Berkeley
A safe place to work, a permit process makers can trust, and land that stays zoned for making. Help them survive; don't zone them out.
The balance and the check
West Berkeley's working and industrial-arts economy is local jobs. First job: put the permit process on the record — every step, its cost, its wait, and who it protects. Then fix the steps the record can't defend.
The balanceRules that protect neighbors against rules that just cost small businesses time — the work is telling them apart, then cutting the second kind.
The checkThe permit record itself — steps, costs, waits — published; break-ins and response times in the maker blocks tracked like anywhere else; and whether the makers are still here, year over year.
Full page →
07What City Hall controls
### Keep Council focused on Berkeley
Council hours are the scarcest resource at City Hall. Mine go to streets, safety, parks, services, and a budget that adds up.
The balance, the check, and where it's been tested
Berkeley has always cared about the wider world, and I share those values. The question is where a councilmember's hours actually change an outcome — the part we control is the part that's been slipping.
The balanceAn evening spent on what Berkeley can't control is an evening not spent on what it can.
The checkThe agenda itself: the share of council time spent on items the city has authority over, published.
Tested: five dates between September and June →Full page →
## Where I stand
The issues Berkeley is arguing about. Each page takes a position, sources every claim to a public document, and lists what I couldn't verify.
All Hot Topics →
Waterfront · District 19 Oct 2026
### Waterfront: recreation first, and a ferry inside the Marina for a fraction of the $105 million pier
Maximize recreation. Make room for travel. Price the in-Marina landing.
Why
Recreation comes first and the ferry fits around it. The current plan is a new 1,080-foot pier and breakwater at about $105 million, with construction unfunded. A landing in the Marina basin next to the hotel uses protected, already-dredged water and has never been priced. Yes to a battery-electric ferry, paid for by WETA, added only as riders show up. Recreation parking stays free with time limits.
Read the full position →
Ballot Measures · Citywide4 Oct 2026
### Measures U, V and Z: no on all three, and what would change that
Show the plan. Price what it costs to run. Then ask.
Why
Seven measures are on the ballot and four are taxes. The $300 million bond lists 31 projects and commits to none of them, and nothing is budgeted to run what it builds. The sales tax is a general tax: permanent, and it promises nothing anyone can check. The bank tax spends $58.3 million over six years on a bank with no charter, and says what happens to the money if it never opens. No on U, V and Z. Yes on W, X and AA; neutral on Y.
Read the full position →
Infrastructure · Citywide4 Oct 2026
### Vision 2050: yes to the plan, and put a year on its targets
Date the targets. Publish the score every year.
Why
In 2022 the Council adopted targets for Berkeley's streets, sidewalks, and bicycle and pedestrian plans, with no year on any of them. The streets scored 56 in 2022 and 56 in 2024, against a target above 70. The Task Force's next steps were due this spring and summer, and I can't find them published.
Read the full position →
Waterfront · District 15 Oct 2026
### Golden Gate Fields: yes to the park, and publish what it costs to open
Buy it. Then publish the cost to open it.
Why
$175 million buys 161 acres of shoreline, 40 of them in District 1. The price includes tearing down the buildings. It doesn't cover the cleanup, building the park, or running it, and none of those costs has been published. Whether to keep the grandstand is still open.
Read the full position →
Streets · District 14 Oct 2026
### Hopkins bike lanes: I'd have voted no — and yes to comparing Ada and Rose first
Compare the two routes, then build.
Why
On July 28 the Council picked a design before anyone laid it beside the alternative. Working up a real route on Ada and Rose and comparing the two lost by a single vote, and it would have delayed nothing — Hopkins isn't due for repaving until 2027–28.
Read the full position →
Procurement · Surveillance4 Oct 2026
### Berkeley never put its surveillance contract out to bid
Bid it, then decide.
Why
Not in 2021, 2023, 2025, or 2026 — through roughly $2 million in proposed spending with one vendor. The City Auditor and the Police Accountability Board have both now put it on the record.
Read the full position →
Policing · Citywide4 Oct 2026
### One tear gas vote. Three separate decisions.
Separate them, and report every use.
Why
Council postponed the vote on September 15 without taking it, and reset it to September 29. The resolution bundles three separable questions: who may use CS gas and under what standard, what returns to crowd settings, and how each use gets reported afterward. The text of each is public.
Read the full position →
Housing · Zoning4 Oct 2026
### Corridor upzoning: keep the neighborhoods we already have
Standards first on San Pablo; no added heights on Solano and College.
Why
SB 79, AB 893 and AB 2011 fix the minimum heights on San Pablo, University and near BART; a Council vote can't undo that. There, the one lever left is design standards — shadow, wind, setbacks, street trees — in force before the applications arrive. On Solano and College no state floor applies, and I'd vote no on the added heights. Tenant and small-business protections go in the ordinance text. Then count what actually gets built.
Read the full position →
Homelessness · Measure P4 Oct 2026
### Berkeley controls 56 of the 320 shelter beds inside Berkeley
Measure it, then fund it.
Why
The county controls referrals to the other 264. The main homelessness fund is projected $22.8 million below zero by 2029, two three-year health plans share no scorecard, and the department running all of it doesn't publish a vacancy rate. Every figure from the City's own Auditor and City Manager.
Read the full position →
Accountability · Health4 Oct 2026
### The city adopted a $36 million health plan with no targets in it
Publish the numbers.
Why
The three-year behavioral-health plan passed on the consent calendar without discussion, the public-health plan's performance measures were published blank, and the one program Berkeley truly measures covers 66 people. Housing has a scorecard; health doesn't.
Read the full position →
Legislation · Planning4 Oct 2026
### The homelessness money: what gets decided next, and when
Five dated decisions between September and June — most on consent calendars.
Why
They will settle the shelter beds, an unprogrammed $14.9 million, and the contracting rules. First chapter: the homelessness and behavioral-health money only. The full city budget gets the same treatment next.
Read the docket →
## Who I am
Full bio →
### Steve Kromer
37 years in Berkeley. My work is measurement and verification — checking whether claimed results were real. I built the Berkeley Transparency Hub, serve on the board of Berkeley Partners for Parks, and volunteer in District 1's parks.
+ More
At Counterfactual Designs I help organizations quantify what their energy and carbon projects really deliver, and I've written a book on the judgment that good M&V demands. I brought that same discipline home to Berkeley by building the Transparency Hub, a public tracker that turns the city's council agendas and contracts into clear, categorized records of where our money goes.
I was honored with the Chris Kindness Award for community service. I'm running because District 1 deserves a councilmember who's measured by results.

// The job
## Berkeley knows how to talk. D1 knows how to work.
"Gets to work" means three things — and all three matter.
It's where Berkeley works — the Gilman maker district, Fourth Street, the University Avenue corridor up to Trader Joe's, the shops along MLK, and the tradespeople and small businesses that give District 1 its character. It's how Berkeley gets to work — North Berkeley BART, safe streets, a commute that functions. And it's a promise: in a city famous for decade-long studies, your councilmember should roll up their sleeves and deliver. Fewer meetings about the work. More of the work.
// The district
## District 1, drawn in one minute.
The whole district, sketched out — the shoreline and the marina, the Gilman and Fourth Street corridors, North Berkeley BART, and the neighborhoods in between.
Your browser can't play this video — download the map video instead.
## The build list
Seven things to get done — in priority order, the way you'd sequence a job, not a wish list.
The standard
### Every item on this list gets the same two questions before it gets my vote.
A council decision is argued three ways, and each carries real information. The job is reading which one the moment actually calls for — and noticing when one of them has crowded out the other two.
LogosWhat does the evidence say? Numbers, records, the staff report’s own footnotes.
EthosWho is asking us to trust them, and what has that trust bought us before?
PathosFeeling — fear on one side, utopia on the other. It tells you what is at stake for people, and it is also how the worst decisions get made: when the fear or the dream is the entire argument and nobody checks it.
Marie Kondo was right about more than closets: a time and a place for everything, and keep what you love. A council calendar is a closet. So before anything below gets my vote, it answers two questions a wish list never does — and you’ll find both spelled out on all seven items.
The balance What is actually being traded here? Not which group wins — what scarce thing we are spending, and on whom.
The check What gets published, so you can tell whether it worked? If I can’t name the record, I don’t yet have a plan.

I've spent years tracking how Berkeley spends its money — I'll bring that scrutiny to the dais and root out waste. Start here: Berkeley Budget Basics — where every tax dollar actually goes. Then see the full department breakdown: six departments, four out of every five dollars.

The check What we funded last cycle set next to what actually got finished — and published results beside every contract: what we paid, what we got. The Transparency Hub standard, applied from the dais.

The same goes for housing: fast, predictable permits for what fits the neighborhood, with the design standards written first so no one needs a decade of design review to find out.

// Why me
## Let's cooperate to plan the work, and work the plan.
My work is measurement and verification — building confidence in results by managing how impact actually gets measured. At Counterfactual Designs I help organizations quantify what their energy and carbon projects really deliver, and I've written a book on the judgment that good M&V demands. I brought that same discipline home to Berkeley by building the Berkeley Transparency Hub, a public tracker that turns the city's council agendas and contracts into clear, categorized records of where our money goes.
I also put in the work on the ground. I serve on the board of Berkeley Partners for Parks, volunteer in District 1's parks, and was honored with the Chris Kindness Award for community service. Parks like Ohlone, Cedar Rose, and James Kenney are where neighbors actually meet — keeping them clean and usable is exactly the kind of unglamorous, get-it-done work I want more of at City Hall. I'm running because District 1 deserves a councilmember who's measured by results, not meetings.
Read my full CV & portfolio →
// Who we are
## When we say "we," here's who we mean.
This isn't a one-person show or a party machine. "We" is a practical, independent coalition across District 1 — renters and homeowners, shopkeepers and tradespeople, parents and longtime neighbors. Not left or right. Just people who'd rather focus on quality of life in our neighborhoods.

// Ranked choice
## Not your first choice? Rank Steve second.
Berkeley uses ranked-choice voting, so you get up to five picks and ranking someone second never hurts your first choice. This is a crowded field of people who care about this city, and I'd rather earn your second-place vote honestly than pretend the others have nothing to offer. If your top pick is someone else, rank them first — then rank me next, and I'll get to work on the streets, the budget, and the services either way.
## Get to work with us.
A District 1 campaign is won at the door and at the drop box. Tell us how you can pitch in — knock, host, donate, or just take a sign.
### One month to go!! Ballots are in the mail.
$10 → $70
One month to go — ballots reach District 1 mailboxes this week, and every dollar goes to reaching voters before they mark a ballot, with the message: integrity and balance. If you live in Berkeley, the city's 6-to-1 match makes your $10 worth $70 to this campaign.
The most any supporter can give is $60. Not $60 from most people — $60 from every single one, with no bundlers and no exceptions. There is no one in this race we'll owe a favor to.
Every dollar, matched or not, gets reported to the city on Form 460 — public on the City Clerk's campaign finance portal, committee #1492682.
Chip in — $10 to $60 →
Takes about two minutes. Berkeley requires a hand-drawn signature on the receipt, so have a finger or a mouse ready.
